dossier.public_summary: The dips vary wildly in depth from one transit to the next and from one TESS sector to the next, with a few unusually deep events creating the apparent period. A steady planet should give the same depth every time, so this is best explained by variable systematic noise or stellar variability, not a planet.

reasons.why: Depths are wildly inconsistent from transit to transit, with a few very deep/shallow events driving the whole signal (97% from top 3). This is not a steady planet transit but a few outliers mimicking a period.
reasons.value: p_consistent=7.562297061551098e-46, share_of_top_3=0.971, chi2=225.33851085592937, outliers: 1126 ppm (sigma 7.8), 702 ppm (sigma 7.5), -7 ppm (sigma -6.1), 574 ppm (sigma 5.1), 84 ppm (sigma -4.4)

reasons.why: Depth really changes within the same pipeline (QLP), from non-detection to 10x deeper, inconsistent with a single-depth planet despite sector-dependent apertures.
reasons.value: verdict changes_within_a_source, p_constant_all=3.8972538944947256e-25, QLP p_constant=3.931749015019587e-06, SPOC 2-min 638±43 ppm (sector 10), TESS-SPOC 162±51 ppm (sector 63), QLP 39±38 ppm (sector 90) vs 359±58 ppm (sector 101)

reasons.why: Extreme sector-to-sector depth variation adds to the transit-to-transit scatter, requiring systematics/blended noise, not a stable planet.
No positive on-target centroid and no large phase signal confirm the dip is not consistently on-target, leaving systematic/variability as the best explanation.
